item.title: In Texas, politicians are treating everyday Muslim practices as a threat
item.description: Some claim that Islam doesn’t really count as a religion and that it is actually a political ideology bent on ‘world domination’.
item.content:encoded:
Elected officials across Texas are increasingly treating ordinary Muslim religious practice – prayer, dress, marriage counseling, even mosques themselves – as evidence of a political threat and saying so openly.

“I won’t rest until every Muslim is gone,” Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, wrote on social media in June. Since late 2025, Texas officials have investigated plans for a Muslim-friendly housing development outside Dallas, as well as a small Dallas organisation that offers religious divorce counseling. Governor Greg Abbott also designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a foreign terrorist organisation under Texas law.

In May 2026 Abbott threatened to pull $530,000 in state funding from Grand Prairie unless the city canceled a private Eid celebration at a water park. He also threatened to withhold funding from Dallas Fort Worth International Airport unless it dropped plans for ablution stations, the washing facilities Muslims use before prayer.

State Representative Alan Schoolcraft, a Republican helping lead the “Sharia Free Texas Caucus”, has framed the distinction explicitly. He told the Houston Chronicle that his concern “has nothing to do with faith, with religion,” but rather with “cultural differences, refusing to assimilate, and trying to establish a parallel culture.”

item.title: Rajasthan HC acting chief justice claims allegations that he misused his office are ‘baseless’
item.description: The judge urged the media and members of the Bar to wait for the decision of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant before arriving at a conclusion.
item.content:encoded:

Justice Sharma said that he had full faith in the judicial system and urged all those concerned to wait for the decision of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant before arriving at a conclusion.

Last month, Supreme Court Justice Sandeep Mehta, in letters to Kant, accused Sharma of manipulating the listing of cases to favour rich litigants and using his position to appoint persons close to him to administrative posts. Mehta had sought that Sharma be replaced with immediate effect.

The Supreme Court collegium on August 31 recommended the appointment of Justice Sanjay K Agrawal as the chief justice of the Rajasthan High Court. Sharma is due to retire on September 26.

item.title: Kenya orders Tata Chemicals to exit country, president says firm failed to benefit local population
item.description: William Ruto said that the Indian company had done little to develop local industries.
item.content:encoded:
Kenyan President William Ruto on Thursday said that he has ordered India’s Tata Chemicals to stop operations in the country, saying that its presence had failed to benefit his country, the BBC reported.

Ruto said that the Indian company had been exporting soda ash instead of processing the mineral locally to produce glass and chemicals. Soda ash, or sodium carbonate, is a chemical that is widely used across industries, especially in glass production.

The Kenyan president made the remarks during a visit to Magadi in Kajiado county, where Tata Chemicals operates a soda ash plant. He said that the company had held a contract for about 100 years but had done little to develop local industries.

“I told them the other day to pack up and leave,” BBC quoted Ruto as saying in Swahili. “They have not built anything in Kajiado, they have not built any factory in Kajiado.”

Tata Chemicals said that it respected the authority of the Kenyan government and remained committed to “constructive engagement through the appropriate legal and regulatory channels to resolve the outstanding matters”, Reuters reported.

item.title: Arunachal: Student activist injured as protest against inclusion of Chakmas in SIR turns violent
item.description: Student groups have demanded that members of the community who arrived in the state after 2006 be not included in the voter rolls.

A student activist was injured in Bordumsa town of Arunachal Pradesh’s Changlang district during a protest against the inclusion of Chakma people who arrived in the state after 2006 in the special intensive revision of voter rolls, India Today NE reported.

A member of the All Arunachal Pradesh Students Union, Khoda Lazer, was injured in clashes between Chakma organisations and student groups, during which stones were thrown. He was taken to a hospital, Northeast Now reported.

Security personnel were subsequently deployed in Bordumsa and adjoining areas to maintain law and order.

The Chakmas and Hajongs were displaced by the construction of the Kaptai Dam in the Chittagong Hill Tracts in Bangladesh in 1957. In the 1960s, the Indian government settled them legally in the territory now known as Arunachal Pradesh.

The violence on Friday took place a day after a hearing on claims and objections at a polling station in Bordumsa was disrupted by members of the students’ union.

The All Arunachal Pradesh Students Union has alleged that bogus names were being included in the electoral rolls, and that this would threaten the identity and interests of the state’s indigenous communities. item.title: Could two moves in Washington torpedo US trade deal with India?
item.description: Bills have been tabled to slap up to 100% tariffs on importers of Russian oil and gas, and generic medicines.
item.content:encoded:
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor recently claimed that the US-India trade agreement is on the verge of finalisation and that “almost everything” about the agreement was done “in principle”.

However, even as Ambassador Gor was exuding confidence regarding the deal, two initiatives taken in Washington in just over a month have brought yet another round of tariff war at India’s doorstep. These initiatives have the potential of increasing friction between the two countries, and could even torpedo the deal.

The most egregious of these developments is theLindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a bipartisan bill tabled in the US Senate, which has the backing of the US President.

This Act proposes imposition of tariffs of up to 100% on all goods from three sets of countries: the five largest importers of Russian crude oil; the five largest importers of Russian natural gas; and countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion.

India, the second largest buyer of Russian crude oil, is an obvious target of the proposed excessive tariffs. This is a continuation of the actions successive US administrations have taken against the Russian Federation since its war against Ukraine.

item.title: A mysterious disease spread like wildfire and killed 29 Adivasi children. What was it?
item.description: Twenty-nine children have died in just one block in Balaghat district.

In July, officials in Balaghat were alerted to the mysterious deaths of three Adivasi children in Bondari, a village in eastern Madhya Pradesh.

“We initially thought it was a seasonal flu. But when we went door to door, we found sick children in every house, ” said the then sub-district magistrate Arpit Gupta.

The kids suffered from fever, their bodies erupted in rashes, and their eyes swelled and turned yellow. The disease, which spread like wildfire across neighbouring villages, killed 29 children in Birsa block.

Humans adapted. It was what they did. Didn’t matter if it was fire, flood, a hurricane hitting your house or your career tanking on account of a string of movies which generated sub-par returns at the box office because the Great American Public could no longer concentrate for a span of time longer than a TikTok reel; the point was that the average human was surprisingly adept at rolling with the punches. It was why, he reckoned, Homo sapiens were still around killing the planet while the Neanderthals and those Hobbit people from Indonesia – he’d forgotten their name – had gone the way of the dinosaur.

item.title: ‘Mirzapur the Movie’ review: Big-screen version of the web series stands on its own bloodied feet
item.description: Director Gurmmeet Singh and writer Puneet Krishna balance fan service with fresh elements.
item.content:encoded:
After three seasons of mayhem on Prime Video, the web series Mirzapur has been transported to the big screen. Mirzapur The Movie harks back to the first season from 2018, when the reign of the drugs-to-guns racketeer Akhandanand Tripathi (Pankaj Tripathi) as the uncrowned king of Mirzapur is challenged within and without.

This is that happy time in the show when Akhandanand, his family, adversaries and political allies are still being introduced one by one. Key characters who eventually perish are very much around. There’s room to joke and spar, unlike in the subsequent seasons, which get serious and heavy and a bit dull as a result.

Gurmmeet Singh, who directed many of the show’s episodes, and writer-creator Puneet Krishna are in firm control of the screen adaptation. Singh and Krishna choose the strongest characters from the sprawling cast, thrown in a few new players, rewrite some of the storylines and blast hip tunes that hop over action scenes.

item.title: Aravallis cannot be defined by height, any single criterion, says SC panel
item.description: The committee has sought time till February to complete the survey and study of the mountain range.
item.content:encoded:
The committee set up to conduct a survey and study of the Aravallis has informed the Supreme Court that the mountain range’s complex landscape cannot be defined using a single terrain or height-based criterion, The Times of India reported on Friday.

It has sought time till February to complete the exercise.

The committee, formed in May, was tasked with defining the Aravallis after the Supreme Court’s adoption of a definition by a Union environment ministry panel led to widespread protests, particularly in Rajasthan. The definition recognised only hills with an elevation of 100 metres or more as part of the Aravallis and was adopted by the court in November.

The court stayed its decision in December amid concerns that the changed definition of the Aravallis could lead to unregulated mining and severe environmental degradation.

In the report submitted to the court, the committee said that it needed to carry out detailed mapping, field inspections, expert assessments and consultations with stakeholders before submitting its final recommendations, The Times of India reported.

“Defining the ancient, and in parts severely degraded, ranges that run between Gujarat and Delhi isn’t an easy task because the Aravallis lack uniformity,” the newspaper quoted the committee as having stated.

item.title: HarperCollins to publish Sonia Gandhi’s memoir ‘Belonging’ in India after Penguin backs out

HarperCollins India will publish Sonia Gandhi’s Belonging: A Journey of Love in the Subcontinent, after Penguin Random House India backed out. William Collins, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers, is also publishing the memoir in the UK. The US edition will be published by Alfred A Knopf, an imprint of Penguin Random House. The memoir will be released globally on November 10.

Last month, The Indian Express reported that Penguin Random House India dropped Gandhi’s memoir as she rejected certain “editorial changes and deletions” that the publisher wanted in the manuscript. PRH India, however, said that any suggestion that it decided not to publish the book because the author declined editorial changes was not accurate.

“As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in the best interests of the book,” it said on social media. “…Throughout the relevant discussions, Penguin Random House India’s position was that we remained willing and keen to publish the book.”

item.title: Step up preparedness for glacial lake outbursts and avalanches, Centre tells Himalayan states
item.description: The directive came after the flash floods on the Nepal-China border on August 26, which led to more than 1,300 deaths.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Home Affairs on Thursday asked states and Union Territories in the Himalayas to step up preparedness against glacial lake outburst floods and snow avalanches.

A glacial lake outburst flood is a sudden release of water from a lake formed by melting glaciers when a natural dam holding it back breaks. Such lakes can form beside, in front of, within, beneath or on the surface of a glacier.

Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan chaired a meeting attended by the chief secretaries and disaster management officials of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, and Jammu and Kashmir, the ministry said.

The meeting came against the backdrop of flash floods on the Nepal-China border on August 26, which led to more than 1,300 deaths. Over 5,000 are missing.

Officials reviewed the risk of glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalayas, focussing on early warning, monitoring vulnerable glacial lakes and snow-covered areas.

The review also focused on identifying high-risk locations and flow paths, timely dissemination of alerts, evacuation preparedness and strengthening response mechanisms.

The Hindi-language film, adapted by Sooni Taraporevala from the Aravind Adiga novel of the same name, stars Manoj Bajpayee in the lead role. Co-produced by Rana Daggubati, the movie will be released on September 11 in cinemas.

Bajpayee plays Yogesh Mishra, a retired school teacher who opposes a proposal to redevelop his decades-old building in Mumbai. Yogesh, who’s also known as Masterji, is increasingly isolated in his stand against the builder Dharmesh Shah (Boman Irani).

item.title: Bengal wants to open 1,000 RSS-run schools in a year, says CM Suvendu Adhikari
item.description: The chief minister also threatened to stop government aid for educational institutes if they refused to sing the full version of ‘Vande Mataram’.
item.content:encoded:
West Bengal wants to open at least 1,000 schools run by Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s education wing Vidya Bharati within a year, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Thursday. The schools would be established in every district, municipality and panchayat, he said.

The RSS is the parent organisation of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Speaking at an event to mark the 74th anniversary of Vidya Bharati in Kolkata, Adhikari also threatened to stop government aid for schools if they refused to sing the full version of Vande Mataram, The Telegraph reported.

“I told them that government aid would stop,” the newspaper quoted him as saying. “Then they budged, but only partially. They stood up, but did not move their lips. Then I told them that lips must move as well.”

The chief minister urged Vidya Bharati to set up more schools in Murshidabad and South 24 Parganas, alleging that “more anti-national activities take place” in the districts, The Times of India reported.

He accused the previous Trinamool Congress government of “polluting” the educational institutions and urged Vidya Bharati to take the responsibility for imparting “nationalistic learning”.

Though India’s struggle for independence was largely non-violent, it was constantly shadowed and vitalised by a relatively small but vocal and, at times, highly effective terrorist movement. The movement began in the 1870s as a reaction against the way in which the colonial government set about responding to the political trauma of 1857.

As we saw elsewhere, most Indians thought that the government in London was sympathetic to their aspirations, but that its good intentions were systematically frustrated by its narrow-minded representatives in India. Queen Victoria’s proclamation seemed to them to indict previous Indian governments and to promise better times. The Raj’s subsequent failure to satisfy the legitimate expectations it had itself aroused led to bitter disappointment. Furthermore, the new style of government in India intensified the growing trend towards bureaucratic rule.

The Indian administrative system was a closed corporation, proud of its professionalism, supremely convinced that it knew how to rule and civilise the country, and held together by a fierce sense of mutual loyalty. It was remote, arrogant, unbending, and in no doubt that it was devoted to the pursuit of the interests of its subjects. item.title: ‘Jagamae Sangeetham’ review: A discordant take on tradition and modernity in classical music
item.description: The Telugu show, starring Prakash Raj, Akshay Lagusani and Sushmita Shetty, is out on Prime Video.
item.content:encoded:
It wasn’t exactly earth-shattering, the conflict between the purity of classical forms and the pandering-to-the-market approach of popular music. Still, the web series Bandish Bandits – a winning title too – managed to drag what was essentially a family-drama-plus-romance over two seasons, hung on the peg of music. And the enduring allure of Rajasthan.

Now, six years later, Palnati Surya Pratap has come up with a Telugu adaptation, Jagamae Sangeetham, replacing the Hindustani classical music backdrop of Jodhpur with a Carnatic setting in Rajahmundry. Straightway, the Prime Video show’s visual variety loses out.

In adapting the original by Anand Tiwari and Amritpal Singh Bindra, nothing has been added to the story. In fact, most of the drama has been flattened to focus mostly on the lead character, Balu (Akshay Lagusani), who’s caught in a tug-of-war between the expectations of his grandfather, Shastri (Prakash Raj), and his pop star beloved, Pallavi (Sushmita Shetty).

Shastri is revered in Rajahmundry and rules the household and his small group of students with unsmiling sternness. He’s unaware of the financial struggles of his older son Sudhakar (Shiju). Nobody tells the old man that his pension has been stopped and that their ancestral mansion is in danger of being auctioned.

Their three children are horrified at the decision to swap creature comforts and gadgets for a bare-bones barn with no electricity, running water or internet access. Tim and Polly want to grow tomatoes; at least two of the children want to hotfoot it back to the city.

Where is the Wi-Fi, the youngest, Joe (Phoenix Laroche), keeps plaintively asking. When handed a copy of Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women, the eldest, Beth (Delilah Bennett-Cardy), scoffs: this is about the oppression of the patriarchy. Also Beth: trees are literally the more boring things in the world.

Only the middle child Fran (Billie Gadsdon) appreciates her new surroundings. Beth has spoken too soon: trees are anything but dull, as the curious and sensitive Fran finds out.

item.title: For months, Adivasi children in Madhya Pradesh kept dying. The government woke up too late
item.description: Scroll travelled to Balaghat to investigate the mysterious outbreak. We found an absent state and lack of healthcare facilities had led to at least 25 deaths.
item.content:encoded:
Mahasingh Parte lives in the last hut in a village on the border of Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

To reach the village, Matla, one has to trek a kilometre up a hill, on muddy trails and slippery slopes.

The village in Balaghat district in eastern Madhya Pradesh is surrounded by rolling hills and forests, a picture of tranquility for tourists visiting the nearby Kanha National Park.

But for Parte and other members of the Baiga tribe, who live in this remote region, life is a daily struggle – with little help forthcoming from the government.

Parte earns a living by collecting and selling tendu leaves and forest produce or labouring on other farms. The hut itself is bare except for a few steel utensils stacked in one dark corner. He grows millet and forages for seeds, other than depending on government ration.

“If we can manage, we eat two meals a day,” he told Scroll. “On many days, my children eat just once.”

In May, Parte’s four-year-old son Samlu caught a high fever. Soon, his six-year-old daughter Shamku’s body also felt warm.

One by one, all his five children fell ill.

item.title: How the US war has changed power equations in Iran
item.description: The fight is no longer about whether to bargain but the precise ways and means of improving Iran’s position before it commits to anything irreversible.
item.content:encoded:
When Washington unveiled its economic “D-Day” on August 19, the latest tightening of the financial siege and the blockade around Iran’s ports, it believed it was applying decisive leverage. But in Tehran the move was read as something else entirely – as confirmation that the US still prefers pressure to any settlement it might one day have to honour.

Across a political system that agrees on almost nothing, the interpretation was remarkably uniform. The economic stabilisers around the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, saw the US as reneging on a deal, while Ahmad Vahidi’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commanders saw their own warnings about American perfidy vindicated.

So whatever faith remained in Iran about US willingness to close a deal has thinned further. That erosion of trust now shapes what Tehran will and will not accept.

It is important to realise that Iran is making existential decisions about the survival strategy of the Islamic Republic itself. The old vocabulary of reformist against principlist – or moderate against hardliner – no longer reflects the real struggle inside the system.

For nearly 40 years, since Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg had planted the first fragile seed of the Lutheran Mission in Tranquebar, Christianity had tried to push its tender roots into the hard earth of the south. item.title: Why Bangladesh should not join the Mecca Pact just to appease Pakistan or send a signal to India
item.description: The three members have pursued their own national interests, often at each other’s expense. Dhaka has no reason to behave differently.

When Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament last week that Dhaka would view an invitation to join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement positively, he framed the country's possible participation as “a measure for the self-defense of the global Muslim community”.

“It is an internal matter of the Muslim family,” Rahman explained.

In India, where the prospect of Bangladesh joining a defence pact founded by Pakistan has drawn considerable attention, that framing has understandably fed suspicion.

For readers on each side of the border, it would be worth trying to understand why the pact's existing members would want Bangladesh in the first place and what Dhaka stands to gain – or lose – by joining in.

The Mecca Pact, signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7, remains a loosely defined arrangement.

Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has called it “purely defensive”, while Türkiye’s Hakan Fidan has likened its core clause to NATO's Article 5, which commits members to mutual defence.

Mechanisms for coordinating senior officials and armed forces are still being developed, and the pact lacks anything resembling NATO's integrated command structure.

item.title: Gloria Steinem, writer and feminist activist, dies at 92
item.description: One of the most prominent voices for reproductive rights, she spent two years in India in the 1950s and said the experience had a ‘huge influence on her’.
item.content:encoded:
Gloria Steinem, American writer and one of the most prominent activists for the reproductive and civil rights of women in the United States, died on Wednesday. She was 92.

She died at her home in New York, her foundation said on social media. “Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” it added.

Steinem started as a journalist in the 1960s, writing a feature on contraception that detailed how women were forced to choose between motherhood and careers. She followed this with an expose on sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at nightclubs owned and operated by Playboy Enterprises.

In 1971, she founded the Ms. magazine, a feminist publication that focused on problems faced by women.

item.title: Gloria Steinem (1934–2026): What we learnt from her 2015 memoir, ‘My Life on the Road’
item.description: One of the globally acknowledged leaders of second-wave feminism, Gloria Steinem died in her New York City home on September 2, 2026 at the age of 92.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published on The Conversation in 2018.

Gloria Steinem’s first book in more than a decade hit bookstores a couple of weeks ago. My Life on the Road proffers autobiographical snippets from what the famed feminist activist, journalist and author claims is the “most important, longest-running, yet least visible part of my life” – her nomadic existence on the road.

Steinem maintains that her intentions in relaying these experiences are manifold. Clearly, she wants to acquaint the public with this lesser-known facet of her itinerant life, but she also declares that she wants to “encourage you to spend some time on the road, too”; for us all “to share stories”; and “to open up the road – literally” given that “so far its been overwhelmingly masculine turf”.

The Supreme Court on Thursday held that the Bar Council of India and state bar councils do not have the statutory power to take disciplinary or punitive action against law students, Live Law reported.

The bar councils get disciplinary powers over law students only after they enrol as advocates, the court said.

It also held that the directions issued by Bar Council of India chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra on August 13 with respect to the graduating batch of students at the National Academy of Legal Studies and Research were unlawful, Live Law reported.

Mishra had directed state bar councils to defer the enrolment of the graduating batch as advocates after the students campaigned against inviting Chief Justice Surya Kant to their convocation over his remarks on police action against youth protesters. The Bar Council of India’s order had also sought an inquiry against the students and faculty members. The council, however, withdrew the directive hours later.

A day after the directive was issued, the Supreme Court had passed an interim order protecting NALSAR students and faculty members from punitive action by the Bar Council of India or any state bar council. Kant had described the bar council’s order as “absolutely uncalled for”.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Longing for an Elsewhere: Mysore and the Making of India’s Developmental State’, by Chandan Gowda.

When the Mysore Representative Assembly (MRA) was founded in 1881, the editorial of a major newspaper published in British India noted:

“A new experiment is being tried in the Mysore state whose progress would be extremely interesting to watch because it has been frequently asserted that Eastern nations are not fitted for such councils or such a Government as that of England or the United States. For many centuries before our time, Hindoos have been despotically governed; so very few of them have actually taken part in the government of their country that they know not what real political freedom and true representative government mean.”

The Census 2027 questionnaire seeking details about the respondents’ parents, spouses and number of bank accounts requires justification from the Union government, said a group of former bureaucrats on Wednesday.

Such information should not be gathered “merely because it can be collected”, the Constitutional Conduct Group pointed out.

The questionnaire for the 2027 enumeration exercise includes 12 questions that were not asked in the previous census. These include questions seeking parents’ names, spouses’ names, permanent residential addresses, their nationality, the place where they got their Covid-19 vaccine, number of bank accounts, mobile phone, and details of Aadhaar, voter ID, passport and driving licence.

“Much of this information appears to have little relevance for generating population statistics or informing public policy,” said the group of retired bureaucrats in an open letter.

This failure is most evident in the functioning of the Office of the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities and its state counterparts, even though they were strengthened as part of the 2016 law to ensure substantive rights and meaningful access to justice for disabled persons.

item.title: How a ‘super El Niño’ could make India’s monsoon drier – yet more dangerous
item.description: It could create an apparently contradictory situation: less rain over the season as a whole, but heavier rain when it does rain.
item.content:encoded:
India is currently in the middle of its summer monsoon, but this year’s rainfall presents an interesting paradox. Much of the country has received less rain than usual so far, yet has still been hit by severe floods and landslides. In Kerala, for example, devastating floods occurred despite the overall monsoon rainfall remaining well below average.

A weaker monsoon does not necessarily mean an absence of extreme rainfall. Rainfall can be highly uneven, with long dry spells broken by intense cloudbursts that cause flooding and landslides. This year’s experience in Kerala illustrates the apparent contradiction: a season that is dry overall can still produce devastating rainfall.

Amid this highly uneven monsoon, attention is also turning to something happening thousands of kilometres away in the tropical Pacific Ocean: El Niño.

It is well established that El Niño years, when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual, are often associated with weaker Indian monsoon rainfall. Meanwhile La Niña – the opposite state to El Niño – tends to favour wetter conditions. This year, El Niño conditions have developed rapidly in the Pacific, with forecasts suggesting it could become exceptionally strong.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday asked the Union government to submit its views on introducing a totaliser system to count votes recorded in a cluster of electronic voting machines, reported Live Law.

At present, votes cast in elections are counted booth-wise. A totaliser would allow votes recorded in multiple machines to be counted together. This can make it difficult to determine how any particular booth voted.

The petitioners in the case have argued that introducing a totaliser system can prevent a candidate or a political party from knowing how much support they received at a particular booth, thereby reducing the chances of post-poll violence, reported Live Law.

They have sought that election results be declared at the parliamentary constituency level, instead of disclosing booth-wise figures separately.

On Tuesday, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the Union government to state if there were hurdles in introducing the system and whether it could have any adverse effects, reported Live Law.

The bench also asked the Election Commission to submit its proposal on the matter to the government.

item.title: More Indian students are abandoning higher education as degrees no longer seem worth the cost
item.description: Political control over educational institutes has lowered the value of academic degrees, which no longer seem worth the cost and time.
item.content:encoded:
While the youth protests were underway at the Jantar Mantar in the first week of July, the Central government published two crucial reports on higher education enrollment: the All India Survey on Higher Education for 2022-’23 and 2023-’24.

The findings were alarming. For the first time since 2011, there has been a decline in the number of Indian students pursuing undergraduate degrees. In 2023-’24, undergraduate enrolment decreased by 93,321 students compared with the previous academic year, representing a decline of 0.29%. This decline at national level might look small. But for a developing country like India enrollments for higher education are supposed to grow fast.

Maharashtra was among the states with the sharpest declines: 5% of Class 12 students here did not enroll in the undergraduate enrollment. This means that nearly 200,000 fewer young people in the state opted for degree programmes compared to the previous year. The number dropped from 35,04,046 in 2023-’24 from 36,88,956 in 2022-’23.

item.title: Mankind destroyed whatever was gifted as life: Tagore’s lament for the environment 87 years ago
item.description: The Nobel Laureate initiated a tree planting festival at Sriniketan on September 2, 1938 when he gave a prescient address, translated into English here.
item.content:encoded:
About a century ago, long before environmental degradation became the crisis of our times, Nobel Laureate Rabindranath Tagore had sounded early warning bells about the destruction of forests.

Though Tagore was born in the city of Kolkata, he had a deep and abiding contact with nature from childhood, and it shaped his many-sided genius in diverse ways. As an adolescent, he accompanied his father Debendranath to the foothills of the Himalayas, an experience he wrote about in his autobiographical notes.

Later, he was a frequent visitor to a zamindari estate in Shilaidaha, now in Bangladesh, where many of his short stories and songs were written while on a boat on the mighty river Padma. He had experienced the vast expanse of nature – in the sky, in the mountains, in the rivers and the flat, verdant lands of the Bengal delta.

Simultaneously he witnessed the urbanisation of the sleepy villages around Kolkata and Kolkata itself, and lamented the oppressive bounds of concrete and the lessening of contact between human beings and nature. item.title: ‘Maxxing’ is just self-care and improvement repackaged for social media
item.description: Constantly focusing on how to maximise ourselves may inadvertently cause us to become more focused on what is wrong with us.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to improve yourself, your health or your lifestyle, you need to do it to the “maxx” – according to social media, at least.

If you want to better your appearance, you need to try “looksmaxxing”. If you want to fix your diet and look after your gut, you should be “fibremaxxing”. And if you want to improve your social skills and be more charming, you really ought to be “personality-maxxing”.

But all of this maxxing might not actually be a good way to motivate yourself into healthier habits. In fact, it may have the opposite effect – and may even cause stress.

The language of “maxxing” has roots in the gaming concept of “min-maxing”, in which players strategically maximise desirable attributes while minimising less useful ones to create the most effective in-game character. The concept then made it’s way to the mainstream, most notably through “looksmaxxing”: making focused, and sometimes extreme, efforts to maximise physical attractiveness.

The suffix has since been adapted in multiple health and wellbeing spaces. If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed.

item.title: How a male Marathi theatre star defined the role of the perfect Hindu wife in the 20th century
item.description: Bal Gandharva’s star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified.
item.content:encoded:
For much of the 20th century, the most admired wife in Marathi-speaking India was not a woman at all.

Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), a celebrated impersonator of Marathi sangeet natak (musical theatre), played devoted heroines with such conviction that film actresses well into the 1970s were trained to reproduce his mannerisms.

How did a man come to define middle-class femininity with such authority?

My recently published research traces Gandharva’s enactment of womanhood from the stage to the marketplace.

It reveals how his star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified – a project that the theatre industry, emerging consumer culture and Hindu nationalist politics each exploited for their own ends.

Staging respectability

India’s pervasive caste system divides Hindus into distinct groups based on which caste they are born into, with certain castes regarded as “higher” than others.

Some of these “lower” castes are made up of hereditary performers: families with a lineage of performing arts. Historically, women from these communities were allowed – and sometimes expected – to perform and entertain.

But Marathi sangeet natak, which emerged in the mid-19th century, was a predominantly upper-caste and middle-class practice.

item.title: Two days after Bhagwat’s speech in New York, 90 US politicians pledge to not take RSS-linked funding
item.description: The signatories include California’s Ro Khanna, who is returning $6,600 that he ‘recently discovered from a pro-MAGA, billionaire with ties to the RSS’.
item.content:encoded:
As Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh Mohan Bhagwat took the stage at New York City’s Madison Square Garden on Saturday to deliver a message of “universal oneness”, a group of nearly 90 American politicians was preparing a different memo: they would not accept political contributions from entities linked to the Hindutva organisation he leads.

The pledge, announced on Monday by Hindus for Human Rights Action and SACRED Acts, commits elected officials and candidates across eight American states to reject contributions connected to the RSS and its affiliates. When the Covid pandemic hit around March 2020, death itself lost its meaning because everyone was dying or was on the waiting list to hell. The wail of the ambulance, too, had lost its meaning because that sound had become the only noise in that deadly silence that had descended on the world. In Delhi, there was no space to bury the mounting dead. There was no farewell unless you treated the honking of the ambulance as a dirge or the drumbeats that herald Yama, the god of death. Bodies were being dumped all over. For a news photographer, it could be heaven or hell. How do you capture the inevitability of people dying in front of you? item.title: August hottest since 1901, September rainfall likely below normal: IMD
item.description: The El Niño conditions that hamper rains are expected to strengthen further in the coming months, said the India Meteorological Department.

Last month was the hottest August since 1901, the India Meteorological Department said on Monday. It also forecast that the rainfall in September will be below normal.

The average temperature across the country was 28.01 degrees Celsius, warmer than the normal of 27.34 degrees Celsius during the month.

The average maximum temperature during the month was 31.66 degrees Celsius instead of the normal of 31.01 degrees Celsius, the weather department said. The average minimum temperature was 24.36 degrees Celsius, higher than the normal of 23.6 degrees Celsius.

In eastern, northeastern and southern India, the average maximum temperature was more than 1.1 degrees Celsius higher than the normal.

September forecast

The weather department also said that the southwest monsoon rainfall in most part of the country will be below normal and less than 91% of the long period average.

The long period average is the measure of the mean rainfall during the four-month monsoon season over the last 50 years.

However, some areas in the northwest, northeast, east, east-central and southeast peninsular India, are likely to receive normal to above-normal rainfall, it said.

The average maximum temperatures are likely to be above-normal in most parts of the country, the India Meteorological Department said.

item.title: When an Indian politician pushed for an anti-communist alliance of Asian democracies
item.description: As India seeks closer cooperation with the US and Asian partners against China, Minoo Masani’s thought is relevant to New Delhi’s strategic posturing.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump’s tenure has vindicated many in the Indian foreign policy establishment prone to reflexive anti-Americanism. However, the recent history of intensified engagement between India and the US, the ongoing bureaucratic collaboration, and the Indian ruling establishment’s cautious reaction to Trump suggest New Delhi’s receptivity to a turnaround in the relationship.

India’s continued insistence on better ties with the US provides an opportune segue to analyse the historical roots of the pro-American, liberal ideational strand of Indian internationalist thought.

Against the backdrop of the Cold War geopolitics, this particular vision offered an alternative to former Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru’s non-aligned, zone of peace approach to the Asian regional security order. Nobody represented the Indian liberal internationalist vision as forcefully as Minoo Masani, the founding leader of the Swatantra party (1959-74).

Based on previously unused archival sources, this inquiry into Masani’s vision for India’s place in the Asian security order highlights a crucial strand of Indian internationalism during the early Cold War years, motivated by a strong sense of both geopolitical and ideological assault by the communist movement.

item.title: Eating pulses can be great for the body, suggests science
item.description: Human trials suggest pulses can reduce blood-sugar rises after meals, modestly improve cholesterol and increase feelings of fullness.
item.content:encoded:
Lentils, beans and chickpeas have been feeding people for thousands of years. Lentils are among the world’s earliest cultivated crops, with archaeological evidence tracing them back to the beginnings of agriculture. Yet scientists are still learning what happens inside our bodies when we eat them.

A 2026 review of the research examined the evidence on pulses and their effects on the gut and metabolism. Pulses are the dried edible seeds of legume plants, including lentils, chickpeas, dried beans and dried peas. Legumes are the wider plant family and also include foods such as soya and fresh peas.

The researchers brought together evidence from human studies with laboratory and animal research. So what does the science suggest pulses actually do once we eat them?

1. They feed microbes in your gut

Pulses provide plant protein and fibre, along with carbohydrates that are not always completely broken down before they reach the large intestine.

There, gut microbes get involved. When some bacteria break down fibre and other carbohydrates, they produce substances called short-chain fatty acids. These help support the lining of the gut and are involved in how the immune system and metabolism work.
